detailedExplanation: Verified against The Tiffin Girls’ School Year 9 Physics Curriculum Outline 2026–27 and aligned to AQA GCSE Physics 8463.
Evaporation is the escape of higher-energy particles from the surface of a liquid. It can occur at temperatures below the boiling point and does not require bubbles to form throughout the liquid.
When the fastest particles escape, the average kinetic energy of the particles left behind decreases. The liquid therefore cools unless energy is supplied from the surroundings.

Evaporation is faster when more particles have enough energy to escape or when escaped vapour is removed from above the surface. Higher temperature, larger surface area and greater airflow generally increase the rate.

Evaporation and boiling are different processes: evaporation occurs only at the surface and over a range of temperatures, whereas boiling occurs throughout a liquid at its boiling point for a given pressure.

Evaporation happens when higher-energy surface particles escape the liquid. It can cool the remaining liquid; warmer conditions, larger exposed surface and moving dry air generally speed evaporation, whereas higher humidity slows net evaporation.
examTips: For cooling explanations, use the sequence: highest-energy particles escape → average kinetic energy falls → temperature falls.
